claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic rod-shaped pathogen that contaminates a wide range of substrates, from very soft tissues to rigid implants.
source: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is an opportunistic rod-shaped pathogen that contaminates a wide range of substrates, from very soft tissues to rigid implants (Moradali et al., 2017; Chang, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Moradali et al., 2017; Chang, 2017).

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is extremely prone to developing antibiotic resistance.
source: A particularly gifted and versatile biofilm-former, it is extremely prone to developing antibiotic resistance (Pang et al., 2019; Boucher et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pang et al., 2019; Boucher et al., 2009).

claim: Type IV pili (T4P) are thin protein filaments on the bacterial surface that can extend and contract by assembly and disassembly of the protein subunit PilA.
source: T4P are thin protein filaments on the bacterial surface that can extend and contract by assembly and disassembly of the protein subunit PilA.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about T4P structure and function.

claim: The tip of T4P acts as a promiscuous hook that can grasp most surfaces.
source: The tip of T4P acts as a promiscuous hook that can grasp most surfaces.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about T4P function.

claim: Attachment, contraction, detachment and extension cycles of T4P propel bacteria.
source: Attachment, contraction, detachment and extension cycles propel bacteria (Merz et al., 2000; Maier and Wong, 2015; Skerker and Berg, 2001; Talà et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Merz et al., 2000; Maier and Wong, 2015; Skerker and Berg, 2001; Talà et al., 2019).

claim: On soft PAA hydrogels (<10 kPa), bacteria form well-defined, dense hemispherical colonies.
source: on the softest hydrogels (<10 kPa), bacteria form well-defined, dense hemispherical colonies
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On stiff hydrogels, bacteria are distributed in a thin layer covering most of the surface.
source: in contrast, on stiff hydrogels, bacteria are distributed in a thin layer covering most of the surface, a morphology closer to what we observe on glass.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bacterial growth rate is not impacted by substrate rigidity.
source: To rule out any effect due to changes in the bacterial growth rate, we quantified the division time of bacteria (Figure 1C), and the volume occupied by bacterial colonies after a few hours (Figure 1D and E) on different substrates: both were found to be unaffected
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The volume occupied by bacterial colonies after a few hours is unaffected by substrate rigidity.
source: To rule out any effect due to changes in the bacterial growth rate, we quantified the division time of bacteria (Figure 1C), and the volume occupied by bacterial colonies after a few hours (Figure 1D and E) on different substrates: both were found to be unaffected
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The characteristic roughness of the bacterial layer decreases as rigidity increases.
source: In contrast, a change in the morphology of the colonies could be confirmed by quantifying the characteristic roughness of the bacterial layer, which decreases as rigidity increases (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The distribution of bacteria with the distance from the surface spreads further for soft hydrogels.
source: and the distribution of bacteria with the distance from the surface, which spreads further for soft hydrogels (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Similar results regarding the phenotype of colonies were obtained on PEG hydrogels, confirming a role for the mechanical properties of the substrate in bacterial self-organization.
source: To control that this is a robust phenomenon driven by substrate elasticity rather than specific chemical interactions, we reproduced this assay using polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels, which are chemically different from PAA but can span a similar range of rigidities. We obtained very similar results regarding the phenotype of colonies, which further confirms a role for the mechanical properties of the substrate in bacterial self-organization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Experiments on hydrogels immobilized at the bottom of wells without agitation showed the formation of denser colonies on softer PAA.
source: Finally, because shear flow can orient polarly-attached bacteria, direct motility, disperse quorum-sensing molecules, and generally impact spatial organization into colonies, we carried out experiments on hydrogels immobilized at the bottom of wells, without any agitation of the above medium. Although long-term observations are rendered difficult in that case by swimming bacteria, we clearly observed the formation of denser colonies on softer PAA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: T4P-mediated surface motility (twitching) plays a key role in the rigidity modulation of microcolony formation by WT PAO1 on soft elastic substrates.
source: We therefore conclude that T4P-mediated surface motility ('twitching') plays a key role in the rigidity modulation of microcolony formation by WT PAO1 on soft elastic substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that pilA mutants do not show rigidity-dependent colony morphology.

claim: Both wspR and sadC mutants exhibited a stiffness-dependent twitching motility.
source: We carried out experiments with wspR and sadC mutants, two DGCs known to be involved in the surface-sensing response. Although impaired in c-di-GMP regulation, both mutants still exhibited a stiffness-dependent twitching motility (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The experimental results on bacterial effective motility on elastic substrates can be interpreted as the result of a simple interplay between the pilus retraction mechanism, the deformation of the elastic substrate, and the friction of the bacterial body on this substrate.
source: Together this demonstrates that our experimental results on bacterial effective motility on elastic substrates can be interpreted as the result of a simple interplay between the pilus retraction mechanism, the deformation of the elastic substrate, and the friction of the bacterial body on this substrate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the agreement between the kinetic model and experimental data.

claim: Track duration is bimodal, with one peak centered on the division time (~27 min) and a second peak corresponding to bacteria spending 5–10 min on the surface before detaching.
source: We expected track duration to be similar to the characteristic division time shown on Figure 1C. However, we obtained a bimodal distribution, with two peaks centered at times unaffected by the substrate rigidity: one peak indeed centered on the division time (∼27 min), and a second one that corresponds to bacteria spending 5–10 min on the surface before detaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The velocity distribution corresponding to each population (short and long tracks) is similar.
source: The velocity distribution corresponding to each population is similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The distribution of the mean velocity of tracks is broad, continuous with an exponential decay.
source: The distribution of the mean velocity of tracks does not allow us to distinguish different bacterial sub-populations: it reaches higher values on stiffer hydrogels, but it is broad, continuous with an exponential decay (reflecting the diversity of behaviors expected in a population of cells; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For each track, the standard deviation of the mean velocity is comparable and proportional to its mean.
source: In addition, for each track the standard deviation of this mean velocity is comparable and proportional to its mean (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting a stochastic distribution of twitching steps within a given trajectory.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Velocity values measured in a given experiment always exhibit a similar dependence on substrate rigidity, showing a clear increase of motility as rigidity increases.
source: However, velocity values measured in a given experiment always exhibit a similar dependence on substrate rigidity, that is a clear increase of motility as rigidity increases.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bacterial motility on PEG hydrogels confirms the very similar bacterial behavior on the two kinds of substrates (PAA and PEG).
source: Finally, this approach was used to quantify bacterial motility in experiments on PEG hydrogels (shown Figure 1—figure supplement 1–pp.), which confirms the very similar bacterial behavior on the two kinds of substrates we have used (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Not only the velocity, but also the contour length of the trajectories of bacteria increases with the rigidity.
source: Our experimental data show that not only the velocity, but also the contour length of the trajectories of bacteria increases with the rigidity since the duration of these trajectories is mostly constant (Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For high stiffness substrates where bacteria explore the surface efficiently, trails of matrix decorate a significant fraction of the surface.
source: For high stiffness substrates where bacteria explore the surface efficiently, this staining confirms that trails of matrix decorate a significant fraction of the surface; on the contrary, nearly immobile bacteria on soft substrates accumulate matrix locally, leaving most of the surface unmodified (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Nearly immobile bacteria on soft substrates accumulate matrix locally, leaving most of the surface unmodified.
source: For high stiffness substrates where bacteria explore the surface efficiently, this staining confirms that trails of matrix decorate a significant fraction of the surface; on the contrary, nearly immobile bacteria on soft substrates accumulate matrix locally, leaving most of the surface unmodified (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: On rigid hydrogels, most of the surface is covered by bacteria-secreted matrix.
source: While on rigid hydrogels, most of the surface is covered by bacteria-secreted matrix, lectin staining on soft hydrogels is only present on compact colonies separated by regions completely devoid of EPS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lectin staining on soft hydrogels is only present on compact colonies separated by regions completely devoid of EPS.
source: While on rigid hydrogels, most of the surface is covered by bacteria-secreted matrix, lectin staining on soft hydrogels is only present on compact colonies separated by regions completely devoid of EPS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: On rigid substrates, high motility promotes mixing of the offsprings of different cells, resulting in a spatial distribution of the two strains close to random.
source: As expected, rigidity-modulated motility impacts the co-colonization of the hydrogels from early stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): on rigid substrates, high motility promotes mixing of the offsprings of different cells, resulting in a spatial distribution of the two strains close to random (a residual correlation between the colour of neighboring cells is always found due to the presence of cells that have just divided).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly immobile cells on soft substrates exhibit strong correlations between neighboring cells, which mostly arise from a single progenitor cell.
source: Conversely, nearly immobile cells on soft substrates exhibit strong correlations between neighboring cells, which mostly arise from a single progenitor cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: On soft substrates, quasi-monoclonal colonies with complete spatial segregation are observed.
source: This striking difference in strain mixing during surface co-colonization is maintained at later stages of biofilm formation: on soft substrates, quasi-monoclonal colonies with complete spatial segregation are observed, while biofilms forming on rigid surfaces exhibit a close-to-random distribution of the two strains at the 10-μm scale (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Biofilms forming on rigid surfaces exhibit a close-to-random distribution of the two strains at the 10-μm scale.
source: This striking difference in strain mixing during surface co-colonization is maintained at later stages of biofilm formation: on soft substrates, quasi-monoclonal colonies with complete spatial segregation are observed, while biofilms forming on rigid surfaces exhibit a close-to-random distribution of the two strains at the 10-μm scale (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Moran's I index quantitative analysis confirms the decisive impact of rigidity on the structure of mixed biofilms.
source: The resulting quantitative analysis (Figure 5B) confirms the decisive impact of rigidity on the structure of mixed biofilms, with potentially far-reaching consequences on the interactions of different strains in multi-species biofilms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase rate of the fluorescence signal is a direct proxy to the expression rate of gene cdrA, and thus to the changes in c-di-GMP level.
source: For this reporter, the degradation rate of gfp occurs over several hours, and its dilution due to growth and division of bacteria occurs at the same rate on all surfaces (see Figure 1C). The increase rate of the fluorescence signal is thus a direct proxy to the expression rate of gene cdrA, and thus to the changes in c-di-GMP level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the properties of the fluorescent reporter and the observation that bacterial growth is the same on all surfaces.

claim: During a first phase of surface colonization, fluorescence remains low on all surfaces.
source: During a first phase of surface colonization, fluorescence remains low on all surfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The fluorescence signal subsequently starts increasing linearly, roughly at the same time for all surfaces.
source: The signal subsequently starts increasing linearly, roughly at the same time for all surfaces (within the uncertainty of fluorescence quantification, that is ≈10 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The linear increase in fluorescence directly translates into a constant production rate of CdrA.
source: This linear increase in fluorescence directly translates into a constant production rate of CdrA that can be compared for the 4 surfaces (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the linear increase in fluorescence shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is a marked increase in CdrA expression with the substrate rigidity.
source: our analysis shows a marked increase in CdrA expression with the substrate rigidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Substrate rigidity influences the twitching motility of individual bacteria.
source: By continuously imaging surface-attached bacteria in situ, we show that substrate rigidity influences the twitching motility of individual bacteria, therefore strongly impacting the process of microcolony formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: The characteristic twitching velocity increases with substrate stiffness (from 0.02 to 0.4 μm/min when rigidity goes from ~3 to 80 kPa).
source: Through two different analyses of the surface motility of the bacterial population, either via the global evolution of the explored area or via the tracking of individual cells, we find that the characteristic twitching velocity increases with substrate stiffness (from 0.02 to 0.4 μm/min when rigidity goes from ∼3 to 80 kPa).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 3D.

claim: A variety of observed phenomena (3D structure of colonies; EPS deposition on the surface; strain mixing during co-colonization) can all derive from a modulation of the efficiency of pili activity by the deformability of soft substrates.
source: Strikingly, our minimal mechanistic model thus suggests that a variety of observed phenomena (3D structure of colonies; EPS deposition on the surface; strain mixing during co-colonization) can all derive from a modulation of the efficiency of pili activity by the deformability of soft substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the agreement between the mechanistic model and multiple experimental observations.

claim: The adaptation of bacterial behavior to the environment can be instantaneous through a purely mechanical model.
source: This purely mechanical model may be of particular importance for surface colonization, since the adaptation of bacterial behavior to the environment can thus be instantaneous - possibly a key to PA ability to efficiently colonize extremely different microenvironments.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the mechanistic model.

claim: Differences in c-di-GMP expression level are detected only 6–7 hr after the onset of surface colonization.
source: While the level of expression of the gene is clearly impacted by the substrate rigidity, differences in expression level are detected only 6–7 hr after the onset of surface colonization, with a first phase characterized by low c-di-GMP level on all surfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The difference in gene expression observed is probably not due to a direct sensing of the substrate rigidity by individual bacteria, but rather a consequence of their organization into more or less dense colonies.
source: This timeframe suggests that the difference in gene expression that we observe is probably not due to a direct sensing of the substrate rigidity by individual bacteria, but rather a consequence of their organization into more or less dense colonies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the timing of c-di-GMP expression changes.

claim: When the increase in c-di-GMP takes place, bacteria have stopped twitching and immobilized into colonies.
source: Of note, when the increase in c-di-GMP takes place bacteria have stopped twitching and immobilized into colonies.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The dense colonies observed on soft hydrogels correspond to lower c-di-GMP levels than the flat bacteria carpets that grow on rigid substrates.
source: The dense colonies observed on soft hydrogels correspond to lower c-di-GMP levels than the flat bacteria carpets that grow on rigid substrates, a somehow counter-intuitive result given the paradigm that c-di-GMP production upregulates biofilm-inducing genes, in particular matrix production, while downregulating motility.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Motility is rendered impossible by the micromechanical properties of the environment rather than by the absence of functional pili on soft substrates.
source: Here, we describe a case when motility is rendered impossible by the micromechanical properties of the environment rather than by the absence of functional pili, thus resulting in the rapid formation of compact colonies on soft substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations that WT bacteria on soft substrates have low motility despite having functional pili.

claim: Rigidity-modulated twitching could provide Pseudomonas aeruginosa with a convenient means of targeting soft tissues for cooperative disruption and subsequent invasion.
source: Recently, Cont et al., 2020 have shown that dense colonies were able to deform soft substrates and exert forces that could disrupt an epithelium layer: rigidity-modulated twitching could thus provide Pseudomonas aeruginosa with a convenient means of targeting soft tissues for cooperative disruption and subsequent invasion.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the current findings and previous work (Cont et al., 2020).

claim: Dense colonies are likely to impact subsequent interactions of bacteria with their environment, including response to changes in nutrient or oxygen availability, and chemical signals.
source: The phenotypic differences that we report for colonies are likely to impact subsequent interactions of bacteria with their environment: response to changes in nutrient or oxygen availability, and chemical signals in general which will not efficiently penetrate inside dense colonies.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypic differences.

claim: The motility modulation mechanism described is quite general and should be marginally affected by the particulars of different strains/species moving through elongation/retraction of an appendage.
source: Since the motility modulation mechanism described here is quite general and should be marginally affected by the particulars of different strains/species moving through elongation/retraction of an appendage, we expect it to provide a relevant framework to study co-colonization in different mechanical micro-environments.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: PAA can span a biologically-relevant range of rigidities (from ~1–100 kPa) while keeping a low viscous dissipation.
source: By varying the amount of bisacrylamide cross-linker during its preparation, PAA can span a biologically-relevant range of rigidities (from ∼1–100 kPa) while keeping a low viscous dissipation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PAA hydrogels.

claim: The gels are spatially homogeneous at the μm and mm scales.
source: Homogeneity of the gels was assessed at the μm and mm scales by multiposition measurements. We found very good repeatability of the measurements and homogeneity of the gels at all scales (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: There is no evidence of damage to the hydrogel upon drying, except for very soft gels of rigidity below 1 kPa.
source: Rigidity was also measured before and after drying and rehydration of the gel to check for possible damage to the structure. In addition, confocal images of the surface of fluorescently labelled gels were used to track default on the gel surface before and after drying. We found no evidence of damage to the hydrogel upon drying, except for very soft gels of rigidity below 1  kPa that were not used in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.
